claims.text: In single-phase bcc refractory high-entropy alloys, percolating SRO clusters cause a nonlinear reduction in thermal conductivity through a percolative scattering transition rather than simple additive scattering.
When the SRO correlation length exceeds the phonon mean free path and the clusters form a connected network, the phonon scattering rate increases super-linearly.
Percolating SRO produces thermal conductivity below the values predicted by serial or parallel mixing models.
A percolating SRO network creates a spatially correlated potential-energy landscape that resonantly scatters mid-to-long-wavelength phonons in addition to mass-difference scattering.
The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy is single-phase bcc, has highly developed percolating SRO, and remains stabilized at high temperature.
Changing the cooling rate can tune SRO cluster size and move HfNbTaTiZr across an SRO percolation threshold.
APT and diffuse X-ray scattering can be used to characterize the SRO correlation length and percolation state.
The alloy remains single-phase bcc during operation at approximately 1000–1500 K.
The percolating SRO network has characteristic length scales comparable to phonon wavelengths.
SRO in a single-phase bcc RHEA produces local variations in atomic mass and bond stiffness.
Isolated SRO clusters act as point defects and scatter phonons through Rayleigh scattering.
Percolated SRO clusters form a continuous network of potential-energy barriers.
Correlated potential fluctuations in the percolated network cause resonant or coherent phonon scattering that is stronger than the sum of individual-defect scattering.
Standard mixing models fail to capture the sharp conductivity drop because they assume uncorrelated disorder.
In MoNbTaW, SRO hinders screw-dislocation motion and can create locking or additional resistance to motion.
The dislocation-pinning behavior of SRO in MoNbTaW is mechanistically analogous to correlated-potential barriers for phonon transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Thermal conductivity will decrease sharply and nonlinearly when the SRO correlation length crosses the percolation threshold.
Measured thermal conductivity will be 15–25% below predictions from standard mixing or simple point-defect-scattering models.
The conductivity reduction will be strongest for phonons whose wavelengths are comparable to the SRO cluster spacing.
A linear conductivity decrease that agrees with an uncorrelated point-defect model and shows no anomaly at the measured percolation threshold would falsify the percolative-transition hypothesis.
